newsitem.title: USA: U.S. business economists see '97 growth, new hiring says survey.
newsitem.headline: U.S. business economists see '97 growth, new hiring says survey.

text.p: Employers have grown more confident about taking on new workers in coming months, reflecting their outlook for steady economic growth in 1997, according to a survey of business economists released Sunday.

In a quarterly survey of 127 members of the National Association of Business Economists, about 42 percent said their companies plan to increase hiring over the next six months. That's up from 24 percent in October's survey.
Roughly half of the economists said they expect the economy to continue growing at an "average" pace, compared with 44 percent in the previous survey.
NABE President Mark Dadd said the survey did not ask for specific growth forecasts but he pegged "average growth" at about 2.5 percent a year.
"This is a pretty solid rate of growth for this stage in the expansion," Dadd told Reuters. "The expansion looks secure."
Another 42 percent of those surveyed forecast sluggish growth, while the rest were evenly split between strong growth and recession.

The survey of the group's members, who include economists from a broad range of U.S. companies, found that demand for products and services increased markedly in the fourth quarter and more than compensated for a third quarter slowdown.
Despite the higher demand, businesses have had difficulty raising prices in a competitive business environment, the survey showed.
Only 21 percent reported increased selling prices for their goods and services, while 14 percent reported falling prices.
Continued shortages of skilled labour were reported at about half of the firms surveyed.
Despite the lengthier expansions of recent years, most of the economists surveyed "still firmly believe in business cycles," the group said.
"Business economists don't believe the business cycle is dead, it's merely slumbering," said the NABE's Dadd, who is also chief economist for AT&T Corp.
